key_terms.meaning: α = (10/L) log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) in dB/km, L in km; link loss A = αL dB; α(Np) = 0.2303 α(dB).
3 dB halves the power, 10 dB divides it by ten; P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW), so 1 µW = −30 dBm.
850 nm (about 2 to 2.5 dB/km), 1310 nm (about 0.35 dB/km), 1550 nm (about 0.2 dB/km); water peak near 1383 nm.
Silica itself: UV electronic tail and IR multiphonon tail; α<sub>IR</sub> = 7.81 × 10¹¹ e<sup>−48.48/λ</sup> dB/km (λ in µm), 0.02 dB/km at 1.55 µm.
Impurities: OH⁻ overtones near 1.38, 0.95 and 0.72 µm (combination band 1.24 µm) and transition-metal ions.
γ<sub>R</sub> = (8π³/3λ⁴) n⁸p²β<sub>c</sub>kT<sub>F</sub>; in practice α<sub>R</sub> = C/λ⁴ with C ≈ 0.8 dB·km⁻¹·µm⁴, 0.14 dB/km at 1550 nm.
Scattering by imperfections about the size of λ; weaker λ dependence, removed by clean fabrication.
Loss of a visible curve, α<sub>r</sub> = c₁e<sup>−c₂R</sup> per turn; rises with λ.
Multimode R<sub>c</sub> ≈ 3n₁²λ/[4π(n₁² − n₂²)<sup>3/2</sup>]; single-mode R<sub>cs</sub> ≈ [20λ/(n₁ − n₂)<sup>3/2</sup>](2.748 − 0.996λ/λ<sub>c</sub>)<sup>−3</sup>.
δT<sub>s</sub> ≈ Ln₁Δ/c, about 49 ns/km for n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01; RMS σ<sub>s</sub> = Ln₁Δ/(2√3 c).
δT<sub>g</sub> ≈ Ln₁Δ²/(8c), about 62 ps/km for Δ = 0.01; optimum-profile RMS σ<sub>g</sub> = Ln₁Δ²/(20√3 c).
B ≤ 1/(2δT) from a full spread; B ≈ 0.2/σ from an RMS width.
D = D<sub>m</sub> + D<sub>w</sub> in ps/(nm·km); spread Δτ = |D|LΔλ in ps; Δλ = λ²Δf/c.
D<sub>m</sub> = −(λ/c) d²n/dλ²; zero near 1270 nm for silica, about +21 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm.
From the change of mode confinement with λ; about −4 ps/(nm·km) in standard fiber; moves the total zero to 1310 nm.
Mean DGD ⟨Δτ⟩ = D<sub>PMD</sub>√L (ps/√km); keep ⟨Δτ⟩ ≤ 0.1 T<sub>b</sub>; beat length L<sub>B</sub> = λ/δn.
DSF has its zero at 1550 nm; NZDSF keeps 2 to 6 ps/(nm·km) to suppress four-wave mixing in WDM.
D₁L₁ + D₂L₂ = 0; DCF at −80 to −100 ps/(nm·km), about 0.5 dB/km; slope match S/D equal for both fibers.
L<sub>eff</sub> = (1 − e<sup>−αL</sup>)/α with α in Np/m; 21.2 km for 80 km at 0.2 dB/km.
P<sub>th,B</sub> ≈ 21A<sub>eff</sub>/(g<sub>B</sub>L<sub>eff</sub>), a few mW, backward, 11 GHz; P<sub>th,R</sub> ≈ 16A<sub>eff</sub>/(g<sub>R</sub>L<sub>eff</sub>), near 1 W, 13 THz.

takeaways: Attenuation is quoted in dB/km so that fiber, splice, connector and bend losses simply add; received dBm = launch dBm − total dB.
Intrinsic absorption belongs to silica itself (UV and IR tails); extrinsic absorption comes from impurities, above all the OH⁻ water peak near 1383 nm.
Rayleigh scattering falls as 1/λ⁴ and the infrared tail rises past 1.6 µm, so the loss minimum, about 0.2 dB/km, sits near 1550 nm.
Bend loss climbs exponentially as the radius falls toward the critical radius, and it is worse at longer wavelengths.
In multimode fiber the spread comes from mode delays: Ln₁Δ/c for step index, about Ln₁Δ²/(8c) for a near-parabolic graded core.
In single-mode fiber the spread is chromatic, Δτ = |D|LΔλ, with D = D<sub>m</sub> + D<sub>w</sub>, zero near 1310 nm and about 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm.
PMD is random and grows as √L; it matters for long links at 10 Gbit/s and above.
Dispersion-shifted fiber moves the zero to 1550 nm, NZDSF keeps a little dispersion for WDM, and DCF cancels the accumulated dispersion of a span.
Stimulated Brillouin scattering limits the power per channel at a few mW; stimulated Raman scattering limits the total power at near 1 W.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for a labelled loss-against-wavelength sketch with the absorption tails, the water peak and the 1/λ⁴ Rayleigh law, and for the intermodal delay formulas of step- and graded-index fibers; numerical questions on dB loss, pulse spread and dispersion compensation are common.

bank.q: Define the attenuation coefficient of an optical fiber. Derive its expression in dB/km and explain why fiber loss is quoted this way.
outline: Define α from P<sub>in</sub>, P<sub>out</sub> and L
Start from exponential decay and convert to dB
Explain why dB losses add along a link
Give typical values in the three windows
answer: Definition. The attenuation coefficient α is the loss of optical power per unit length of fiber. If Pin is launched into a fiber of length L km and Pout leaves the far end, α = (10/L) log₁₀(Pin/Pout) dB/km. Both powers must be in the same unit.

answer.text: Derivation. Each short length dz removes the same fraction of the power that reaches it, so dP/dz = −α′P, where α′ is the coefficient in nepers per unit length. Integrating:
answer.pre:
P(L) = P<sub>in</sub> e<sup>−α′L</sup>
ln(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) = α′L
10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) = 10 log₁₀(e) × α′L = 4.343 α′L
α (dB/km) = (10/L) log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) = 4.343 α′ (per km)

answer: Why decibels. A link is a chain of sections, each passing a fraction of the power: Pout = Pin × T₁ × T₂ × T₃… The logarithm turns this product into a sum, so the loss in dB of the whole link is the sum of the losses of fiber, splices, connectors and bends. With powers in dBm (decibels relative to 1 mW) the received power is simply the launch power minus the total loss.
Why per kilometre. The fiber loss grows in proportion to length, so one number α describes a fiber of any length: A = αL. A designer reads the reach directly: allowed loss ÷ α.
A worked line. 1 mW (0 dBm) into 80 km at 0.2 dB/km: A = 0.2 × 80 = 16 dB, so Pout = −16 dBm = 1 mW × 10−1.6 = 25.1 µW.
Check. Convert back: 10 log₁₀(1 mW/0.0251 mW) = 10 × 1.600 = 16.0 dB, the same loss. And 0.2 dB/km × 0.2303 = 0.046 Np/km, matching α′ = α/4.343.

bank.q: Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic absorption in silica fibers. Name the wavelengths where each is serious and estimate the infrared absorption at 1.55 µm and 1.70 µm.
outline: Intrinsic: UV electronic tail and IR multiphonon tail of SiO₂
Extrinsic: OH⁻ overtones near 1.38, 0.95, 0.72 µm (and 1.24 µm) and metal ions
Use α<sub>IR</sub> = 7.81 × 10¹¹ e<sup>−48.48/λ</sup> dB/km
Remedies: purification, dried preforms, low-water-peak fiber
answer: Absorption turns light into heat inside the glass. It is split by its cause.

Intrinsic absorption belongs to pure silica and cannot be removed by purification. (a) The ultraviolet tail: photons with enough energy lift electrons across the band gap of SiO₂; the edge of this absorption trails toward the visible and falls as λ rises. (b) The infrared tail: the Si–O bond vibrates near 9 µm and a photon can excite several vibration quanta at once (multiphonon absorption); this tail rises steeply beyond about 1.6 µm.

answer.text: Infrared tail, worked. With αIR = 7.81 × 10¹¹ e−48.48/λ dB/km and λ in µm:

answer: The IR term grows sixteenfold between 1.55 and 1.70 µm. The ultraviolet tail of a 6 % germania core is about 0.029 dB/km at 1.55 µm, so intrinsic absorption at 1.55 µm totals about 0.05 dB/km, below the 0.14 dB/km Rayleigh loss.

Extrinsic absorption comes from impurities. Transition-metal ions (Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Cr³⁺, Ni²⁺, V³⁺) give broad bands in the visible and near infrared; vapour-phase preform processes cut them to parts per billion, so they no longer matter in silica fiber.

The hydroxyl ion OH⁻ remains. Its fundamental vibration is near 2.73 µm; overtones fall at about 1.38 µm (the strongest, the water peak), 0.95 µm and 0.72 µm, and a combination band with the Si–O vibration sits near 1.24 µm. Hydrogen entering a cable can create new OH⁻ over the years.

Where each is serious. Below about 0.8 µm the UV tail and the 0.72 µm OH⁻ peak add up; near 1383 nm the water peak dominates in older fiber (about 1 dB/km or more); beyond 1.6 µm the IR tail dominates.

Remedies. Purify the source chemicals, dry the preform with chlorine to remove OH⁻ (low-water-peak fiber cuts the 1383 nm loss to about the 1310 nm level), and choose the 1310 nm or 1550 nm windows that avoid the bands.
Check. At 1.55 µm the intrinsic total (0.049 dB/km) plus Rayleigh (0.14 dB/km) gives about 0.19 dB/km, the familiar 0.2 dB/km loss of single-mode fiber.

bank.q: Explain Rayleigh scattering loss in an optical fiber and show why it falls as 1/λ⁴. Estimate the Rayleigh loss of silica at 0.85 µm and 1.55 µm, and compare it with Mie scattering.
outline: Origin: frozen density and composition fluctuations far smaller than λ
Dipole radiation gives the 1/λ⁴ law
γ<sub>R</sub> = (8π³/3λ⁴) n⁸p²β<sub>c</sub>kT<sub>F</sub> with numbers
Mie: defects about the size of λ, weaker λ dependence, removed by fabrication
answer: Origin. Glass is a frozen liquid. As the fiber cools on the draw tower, density and composition fluctuations freeze in on a scale far smaller than the wavelength. The refractive index therefore varies slightly from point to point.

Mechanism and the 1/λ⁴ law. The optical field polarises each small region, which re-radiates like a tiny dipole. The radiated field of a dipole is proportional to the second time derivative of its moment, so to ω² or 1/λ²; the radiated power is the square, so it scales as 1/λ⁴. Light radiated outside the acceptance angle leaves the core and is lost to the link.

answer.pre:
γ<sub>R</sub> = (8π³/3λ⁴) n⁸ p² β<sub>c</sub> k T<sub>F</sub>     (m⁻¹)
loss over L = 4.343 γ<sub>R</sub>L  dB

answer: Here n is the refractive index, p the photoelastic coefficient, β<sub>c</sub> the isothermal compressibility, k Boltzmann’s constant and T<sub>F</sub> the fictive temperature at which the structure froze.

answer.text: Numbers for silica (n = 1.46, p = 0.286, βc = 7 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/N, TF = 1400 K):

answer: Consequences. Rayleigh loss is the main loss of modern fiber from about 0.8 to 1.6 µm and sets the floor near 1.55 µm. It can be lowered but not removed: slower cooling or annealing lowers TF, and less dopant reduces the composition term; pure-silica-core fiber reaches about 0.15 dB/km in total.

Mie scattering comes from imperfections comparable to the wavelength: core–cladding boundary roughness, bubbles, strain and diameter fluctuations. It scatters mainly forward and depends on λ more weakly than Rayleigh (a 1/λ² model drops only 2.4 times from 1 to 1.55 µm, against 5.8 times for Rayleigh). It is a fabrication defect, cut by good preform making, a smooth interface and a larger index difference.
Check. The ratio of the two Rayleigh results is 1.57/0.142 = 11.06 = (1.55/0.85)⁴, the 1/λ⁴ law.

bank.q: Explain bending losses in optical fibers. Distinguish macrobending from microbending, give the critical bend radius, and say why bend loss is worse at 1550 nm than at 1310 nm.
outline: Macrobending: radiation caustic, exponential loss per turn
Critical radius for multimode and single-mode fibers with numbers
Microbending: random axial distortions, cabling, cures
Wavelength dependence and bend-insensitive fiber
answer: Macrobending is loss caused when the whole fiber follows a curve of radius R. Consider the mode field turning round the centre of the bend. To keep its phase front plane, the field further from the centre must move faster. Beyond a certain distance, the radiation caustic, it would have to exceed c/n₂, the speed of light in the cladding; that part of the field cannot follow the bend and radiates away. A tighter bend brings the caustic closer to the core, where the field is stronger, so the loss rises exponentially: αr = c₁e−c₂R per turn, with c₁ and c₂ fitted to measurements.

answer.text: Critical radius, multimode. Rc ≈ 3n₁²λ/[4π(n₁² − n₂²)3/2]. For n₁ = 1.48, n₂ = 1.46, λ = 0.85 µm:
Critical radius, single-mode. Rcs ≈ [20λ/(n₁ − n₂)3/2](2.748 − 0.996λ/λc)−3. For n₁ = 1.465, n₂ = 1.460, λc = 1.26 µm:

answer: Microbending is loss from many tiny random bends of the fiber axis, with periods of a millimetre or less, caused by uneven coating, cabling pressure, rough drums and thermal contraction of the coating in the cold. Together they couple the guided mode to radiation modes all along the cable, so microbend loss appears as extra dB/km. Cures: a soft inner and stiff outer coating, loose-tube cable design, and care in cabling.

Wavelength. At 1550 nm the mode field is wider than at 1310 nm, so more of it lies beyond the caustic, and the critical radius is larger (24.8 mm against 14.8 mm in the table). Installers therefore check bends at 1550 or 1625 nm. Bend-insensitive fiber adds a low-index trench that pulls the mode inward.
In a budget. Macrobend loss is per turn: four turns at 5 mm of a fiber with αr = 8e−0.6R dB cost 4 × 0.398 = 1.59 dB, as much as 8 km of fiber at 0.2 dB/km.
Check. The two single-mode radii scale by 24.8/14.8 = 1.68: 1.18 from the λ factor (1.55/1.31) times 1.42 from the bracket (0.283/0.199).

bank.q: Define intermodal dispersion and chromatic dispersion. State the unit in which each is quoted, the fibers in which each occurs, and give one number for each.
outline: Intermodal: different mode delays; ns/km; multimode only
Chromatic: group velocity varies with λ; D in ps/(nm·km); all fibers
Chromatic = material + waveguide
PMD as a third mechanism in single-mode fiber
answer: Dispersion is the spreading of a light pulse in time as it travels. A spread pulse overlaps its neighbours and limits the bit rate.

Intermodal dispersion. In a multimode fiber the pulse power is shared among many modes, and each mode (or ray) takes a different time to cross the fiber. In a step-index fiber the axial ray takes Ln₁/c and the steepest guided ray Ln₁²/(cn₂), so δTs ≈ Ln₁Δ/c. It is quoted as a delay per length, in ns/km, or as a bandwidth–length product in MHz·km. It exists only in multimode fiber.

Chromatic (intramodal) dispersion. Within one mode, the different wavelengths of the source spectrum travel at different group velocities. It is described by the coefficient D = (1/L) dτ/dλ in ps/(nm·km), and the spread is Δτ = |D|LΔλ in ps. It occurs in every fiber, single-mode included.

Chromatic dispersion has two parts: material dispersion D<sub>m</sub> = −(λ/c) d²n/dλ² from the glass, and waveguide dispersion D<sub>w</sub> from the change of mode confinement with λ. In standard fiber they cancel near 1310 nm.
A third mechanism. Polarization mode dispersion comes from the two polarizations of the single mode travelling at slightly different speeds; it is random and grows as √L.

Why it matters. Each spread sets a bit-rate ceiling through B ≤ 1/(2 × spread). The 49.3 ns of one kilometre of step-index fiber allows only 1/(2 × 49.3 ns) = 10.1 Mbit/s, while the 170 ps of the single-mode example allows 1/(2 × 170 ps) = 2.94 Gbit/s. This is why multimode step-index fiber is used only for short, slow links, and why single-mode fiber with a narrow laser carries long-haul traffic.

How each is reduced. Intermodal dispersion falls by grading the core index (about Δ/8 of the step value) and vanishes in single-mode fiber. Chromatic dispersion falls with a narrower source, by working near the zero-dispersion wavelength, by dispersion-shifted fiber, or by adding compensating fiber.
Check of units. Intermodal: m ÷ (m/s) = s. Chromatic: ps/(nm·km) × km × nm = ps. Both give a time, as a spread must.

bank.q: A 12 km link uses fiber with α = 0.5 dB/km and has two splices of 0.1 dB each. The launched power is 1 mW. Find the total loss, and the received power in dBm and in mW.
outline: Fiber loss αL
Add the splice losses in dB
Convert the launch power to dBm and subtract
Convert back to mW and check
answer: Given. L = 12 km, α = 0.5 dB/km, two splices of 0.1 dB, Pin = 1 mW.
Fiber loss. Afiber = αL = 0.5 dB/km × 12 km = 6.0 dB.
Splice loss. Asplice = 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 dB.
Total loss. 6.0 + 0.2 = 6.2 dB. Losses in dB add because the transmissions of the sections multiply.
Received power in dBm. 1 mW = 10 log₁₀(1/1) = 0 dBm, so Pout = 0 − 6.2 = −6.2 dBm.
In mW. Pout = 1 mW × 10−6.2/10 = 10−0.62 mW = 0.240 mW = 240 µW.
Comment. 0.5 dB/km is a typical cabled loss near 1310 nm with some excess; at 1550 nm (0.2 dB/km) the same link would lose only 2.4 + 0.2 = 2.6 dB and deliver 0.55 mW.

Margin. Suppose the receiver needs −30 dBm. The margin is −6.2 − (−30) = 23.8 dB. Keeping a 3 dB safety margin for ageing and repairs leaves 20.8 dB, which at 0.5 dB/km would allow 20.8 ÷ 0.5 = 41.6 km more fiber; the link is far from its loss limit.

Why the splices are added in dB. Each splice passes a fixed fraction of the light, 10−0.01 = 0.977 for 0.1 dB, whatever power arrives. Multiplying fractions is the same as adding their dB values, so the order of fiber and splices does not change the result.
Common slip. Adding 6 dB to 0.2 dB/km-style numbers, or converting 6.2 dB to a power ratio of 6.2, would give nonsense; the conversion is always 10−A/10.
Check. 10 log₁₀(1/0.240) = 10 × 0.620 = 6.20 dB, equal to the total loss.

bank.q: A multimode fiber has n₁ = 1.48 and Δ = 0.01. For a 1 km length find the intermodal delay difference and the bit-rate limit B ≤ 1/(2δT) for (a) a step-index core and (b) a near-parabolic graded core. Also find the RMS broadening of the step-index fiber and its limit from B ≈ 0.2/σ.
outline: Step index δT = Ln₁Δ/c
Graded index δT = Ln₁Δ²/(8c)
Bit-rate limits from 1/(2δT)
RMS width Ln₁Δ/(2√3 c) and 0.2/σ
Compare and comment
answer: Common factor. Ln₁/c = 1000 × 1.48 ÷ 3 × 10⁸ = 4.933 × 10⁻⁶ s, the transit time of the axial ray.
The exact form (Ln₁²/cn₂)Δ with n₂ = 1.4652 gives 49.8 ns; the approximation is within 1 %.

Comment. The graded core is better by 8/Δ = 800 in full spread. Both spreads grow with L, so at 2 km every limit halves; this is why multimode fiber is rated by a bandwidth–length product. In practice profile errors and the source’s chromatic spread keep real graded fibers below 8 Gbit/s·km.

Assumptions. The near-parabolic result assumes the profile is close to its optimum at the working wavelength and that all modes carry equal power; the RMS result assumes the arrival times are spread evenly between the two extremes. Both ignore the chromatic spread of the source, which adds in quadrature.

Use in design. A 100 Mbit/s link with B ≤ 1/(2δT) needs δT ≤ 5 ns. On the step-index fiber that allows 5 ns ÷ 49.3 ns/km = 0.101 km, about 100 m. On the graded fiber the intermodal limit alone would allow 5 ns ÷ 61.7 ps/km = 81 km, so in practice loss and chromatic dispersion, not modal delay, set the reach.
Check. 49.3 ns ÷ 61.7 ps = 799 ≈ 8/Δ = 800; and σs = δTs/(2√3) = 49.3/3.464 = 14.2 ns, as a rectangular spread requires.

bank.q: A standard single-mode link is 80 km long at 1550 nm with D = 17 ps/(nm·km). (a) Find the pulse spread for a source of 1 nm spectral width and the limit B ≤ 1/(2Δτ). (b) Repeat for a DFB laser of 0.1 nm. (c) What spectral width, in nm and in GHz, would allow 10 Gbit/s, and what does that imply?
outline: Δτ = |D|LΔλ for each source
Bit-rate limit from 1/(2Δτ)
Required Δλ for 10 Gbit/s and Δf = cΔλ/λ²
Conclusion: dispersion management needed
answer: Given. L = 80 km, D = 17 ps/(nm·km), λ = 1550 nm, rule B ≤ 1/(2Δτ).
At 10 Gbit/s the bit period is 100 ps, so a 1360 ps spread covers more than 13 bit periods: the link fails completely.

answer.text: (c) Width needed for 10 Gbit/s. The rule needs Δτ ≤ 1/(2 × 10¹⁰) = 50 ps.

answer: What it implies. A 10 Gbit/s signal itself occupies roughly 10 to 20 GHz of spectrum, far more than 4.6 GHz, even with an ideal laser. So 80 km of standard fiber at 10 Gbit/s cannot work on spectral narrowing alone. The fixes are dispersion-compensating fiber (17 × 80 = 1360 ps/nm to cancel, for example 16 km at −85 ps/(nm·km)), dispersion-shifted or NZDSF line fiber, moving to 1310 nm where D ≈ 0, or a coherent receiver that undoes dispersion digitally.

Dispersion-limited length. A direct-detection receiver at 10 Gbit/s tolerates roughly 1000 ps/nm of accumulated dispersion. With D = 17 ps/(nm·km) that is about 1000 ÷ 17 = 59 km, so an 80 km span is beyond the limit whatever laser is used.

Moving to 1310 nm. Near 1310 nm, D is below 1 ps/(nm·km), so even the 1 nm source spreads by less than 80 ps over 80 km. The price is loss: 0.35 × 80 = 28 dB instead of 0.2 × 80 = 16 dB, and no erbium amplifier works there.

Compensating at 1550 nm. With DCF at −85 ps/(nm·km), the 1360 ps/nm of the span needs 1360 ÷ 85 = 16 km, which adds 16 × 0.5 = 8 dB of loss; the total 16 + 8 = 24 dB is still below the 28 dB of the 1310 nm option.
Check. Each limit times its spread gives 1/2: 368 × 10⁶ × 1.36 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.50, and 3.68 × 10⁹ × 136 × 10⁻¹² = 0.50.

bank.q: A fiber has a PMD coefficient of 0.5 ps/√km. Find the mean DGD over 100 km and judge the link at 10 Gbit/s and at 40 Gbit/s using the rule ⟨Δτ⟩ ≤ 0.1 T<sub>b</sub>. What is the longest link at each rate?
outline: ⟨Δτ⟩ = D<sub>PMD</sub>√L
Bit periods and the 10 % limits
Maxwellian tail
Maximum lengths from L ≤ (0.1T<sub>b</sub>/D<sub>PMD</sub>)²
answer: Given. DPMD = 0.5 ps/√km, L = 100 km.
Mean DGD. ⟨Δτ⟩ = 0.5 × √100 = 0.5 × 10 = 5.0 ps. The √L law comes from the random rotation of the principal axes along the cable: section delays add like a random walk.

Tail. The instantaneous DGD is Maxwellian. At 10 Gbit/s the limit of 10 ps is twice the mean; the DGD exceeds twice its mean 1.7 % of the time, so even this link sees PMD error bursts for about 6 days a year in total. At 40 Gbit/s the mean already exceeds the limit.

Judgement. The fiber is old (modern fiber is 0.1 ps/√km or less). It works at 10 Gbit/s over 100 km with some outage risk, and is useless at 40 Gbit/s beyond 25 km unless the receiver compensates PMD, as coherent receivers do.

Scaling. Because the mean DGD grows only as √L, quadrupling the length doubles it: 400 km of this fiber gives 0.5 × 20 = 10 ps. Halving the coefficient to 0.25 ps/√km would quadruple the reach at every bit rate.

What can be done. Measure the installed cable before an upgrade (old cable varies a lot from section to section), replace the worst sections, use an optical PMD compensator that tracks the principal states, or use a coherent receiver that undoes PMD in its signal processing.
Check. At the 10 Gbit/s maximum, 0.5 × √400 = 0.5 × 20 = 10 ps = 0.1 Tb; at the 40 Gbit/s maximum, 0.5 × √25 = 2.5 ps = 0.1 Tb.

bank.q: A 100 km span of standard fiber has D = +17 ps/(nm·km), slope 0.058 ps/(nm²·km) and loss 0.2 dB/km. Find the length of DCF with D = −100 ps/(nm·km) and 0.5 dB/km that cancels the dispersion at 1550 nm, the span loss, and the residual dispersion at 1530 and 1565 nm if the DCF slope is −0.10 ps/(nm²·km). What slope would cancel the whole band?
outline: D₁L₁ + D₂L₂ = 0 gives L₂
Loss of fiber plus DCF
Residual at band edges with D(λ) = D + S(λ − 1550)
Slope matching S/D equal
answer: Given. Line: L₁ = 100 km, D₁ = +17, S₁ = 0.058, α₁ = 0.2 dB/km. DCF: D₂ = −100, S₂ = −0.10, α₂ = 0.5 dB/km.
Loss. 0.2 × 100 + 0.5 × 17 = 20 + 8.5 = 28.5 dB. The DCF cancels dispersion, not loss: an amplifier must make up the extra 8.5 dB, and the DCF’s small core (about 20 µm²) adds nonlinearity.

answer.text: Residual at the band edges. Each fiber has D(λ) = D(1550) + S(λ − 1550).

answer: Effect. With a 0.1 nm source, 82 ps/nm gives an 8.2 ps spread, harmless at 10 Gbit/s; but over ten spans the residuals add to 820 ps/nm at 1530 nm, close to the 1000 ps/nm tolerance at 10 Gbit/s and far beyond it at 40 Gbit/s.

answer.text: Slope matching. The residual is zero at every λ when the relative slopes match, S₂/D₂ = S₁/D₁:

answer: Alternatives. NZDSF line fiber keeps D small so the accumulated dispersion is less; dispersion-shifted fiber is avoided in WDM because of four-wave mixing; coherent receivers compensate digitally.

Why DCF is lossy and nonlinear. A large negative D needs a small core and a high germania content, so the fiber has more Rayleigh scattering and more bend sensitivity (about 0.5 dB/km) and an effective area of about 20 µm², four times smaller than standard fiber; the DCF is usually placed between the two stages of an amplifier so its loss does not hurt the noise figure.

Comparison with NZDSF. If the 100 km line were NZDSF at +4 ps/(nm·km), the span would collect only 4 × 100 = 400 ps/nm, within a 1000 ps/nm tolerance at 10 Gbit/s with no DCF at all; the cost is a smaller effective area than standard fiber.

Multi-span links. Over ten such spans the uncompensated residuals add: 10 × (−82) = −820 ps/nm at 1530 nm and 10 × 61.5 = 615 ps/nm at 1565 nm, which is why long links use slope-matched DCF or a final trimming module.
Check. Total at 1550 nm: 1700 + 17 × (−100) = 0. Loss check: 28.5 dB − 20 dB = 8.5 dB = 17 km × 0.5 dB/km.

bank.q: Compare pulse broadening in multimode step-index and graded-index fibers. Derive the step-index delay, explain why the graded profile reduces the spread so strongly, and evaluate both for Δ = 0.01 and Δ = 0.02.
outline: Ray picture: axial and critical-angle rays, δT = Ln₁Δ/c
Graded profile n(r) and the speed–path compensation
δT ≈ Ln₁Δ²/(8c); RMS forms and the 10/Δ factor
Table for two values of Δ
Practical limits
answer: Step-index derivation. The core index is uniform, so all rays travel at c/n₁ and only their paths differ.

answer.pre:
axial ray:       t<sub>min</sub> = L n₁ / c
steepest ray:    meets the boundary at the critical angle, sin φ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁
                 path = L / sin φ<sub>c</sub> = L n₁/n₂
                 t<sub>max</sub> = (L n₁/n₂)(n₁/c) = L n₁² / (c n₂)
δT<sub>s</sub> = t<sub>max</sub> − t<sub>min</sub> = (L n₁²/c n₂)(n₁ − n₂)/n₁ = (L n₁²/c n₂) Δ ≈ L n₁ Δ / c

answer: Graded profile. n(r) = n₁[1 − 2Δ(r/a)α]1/2 for r < a. A ray that swings far from the axis travels a longer, curved path, but most of it lies in lower-index glass where the speed c/n(r) is higher. With α near 2 the extra speed nearly cancels the extra path, so the residual difference is second order in Δ: δTg ≈ Ln₁Δ²/(8c). (Some books quote Ln₁Δ²/(2c) for an exactly parabolic profile by another ray method; the order is the same.)
RMS forms. σs = Ln₁Δ/(2√3 c) and, for the optimum profile α ≈ 2 − 12Δ/5, σg = Ln₁Δ²/(20√3 c). The ratio σs/σg = 10/Δ.

Analysis. Doubling Δ doubles the step-index spread but quadruples the graded spread, so the advantage of grading is largest for small Δ. A large Δ is still chosen for multimode fiber because it raises the numerical aperture and makes coupling from LEDs and VCSELs easy and bending tolerant.

Practical limits. The optimum profile depends on wavelength (profile dispersion), so a fiber optimised at 850 nm is worse at 1300 nm. Small errors in α, a dip or a spike of index on the axis, and differential mode attenuation spoil the cancellation. Real graded fiber reaches a few hundred MHz·km to a few GHz·km, not the ideal 8 Gbit/s·km.

Conclusion. Step index suits short, cheap links of tens of Mbit/s; graded index carries Gbit/s over hundreds of metres in data centres; beyond that, single-mode fiber removes intermodal dispersion completely.

Bandwidth–length product. With B ≤ 1/(2δT) and δT ∝ L, the products are 10.1 Mbit/s·km for step index and 8.1 Gbit/s·km for graded index at Δ = 0.01. A 100 Mbit/s link can therefore run about 100 m on the step-index fiber, against tens of kilometres on the ideal graded fiber.

A figure to draw. Sketch two cores side by side: in the step core a straight axial ray and a zig-zag ray bouncing at the critical angle; in the graded core a straight axial ray and a smooth sinusoidal ray that bends back before reaching the cladding. Label the delays 49.3 ns and 61.7 ps per kilometre.
Check. 98.7/49.3 = 2.0 (∝ Δ) and 246.7/61.7 = 4.0 (∝ Δ²), as the formulas require.

bank.q: Why is 1550 nm the preferred window for long-haul links even though standard fiber has its zero-dispersion wavelength near 1310 nm? Evaluate the loss and dispersion of a 100 km span in each window and discuss how the trade-off is resolved.
outline: Loss mechanisms against wavelength: Rayleigh, IR tail, water peak
Span loss at 1310 and 1550 nm
Dispersion at each window, D = D<sub>m</sub> + D<sub>w</sub>
Amplifiers at 1550 nm
Resolutions: DSF, NZDSF, DCF, coherent DSP; FWM penalty
Judgement with numbers
answer: Loss against wavelength. Rayleigh scattering falls as 1/λ⁴ (about 0.27 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.14 dB/km at 1550 nm for C = 0.8 dB·km⁻¹·µm⁴). The infrared multiphonon tail is negligible at 1310 nm, about 0.02 dB/km at 1550 nm, and rises steeply beyond 1600 nm. The water peak near 1383 nm lies between the two windows. So the loss minimum, about 0.2 dB/km, is near 1550 nm.

Dispersion against wavelength. Material dispersion of silica crosses zero near 1270 nm and reaches about +21 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm. Waveguide dispersion of a standard step-index fiber is about −4 ps/(nm·km). Their sum is zero near 1310 nm and about +17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm.

answer.text: A 100 km span in each window (0 dBm launch, 0.1 nm source):

answer: Near 1310 nm the slope formula gives D(1300) = −0.93 and D(1320) = +0.91 ps/(nm·km), so a 100 km span collects under 100 ps/nm. At 1550 nm the 15 dB loss saving per 100 km is the decisive gain: amplifier spans of 80 to 100 km instead of about 55 km.

The amplifier argument. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers amplify the whole 1530 to 1565 nm band at once, so many WDM channels share one amplifier. Once amplification is cheap, loss sets the spacing of amplifier sites and dispersion becomes a design problem to solve, not a wall.

Resolutions. (1) Dispersion-shifted fiber: a small core and large Δ make Dw about −21 ps/(nm·km), moving the zero to 1550 nm; ideal for one channel, but in WDM every channel travels in step and four-wave mixing grows. (2) NZDSF: 2 to 6 ps/(nm·km) across the band keeps channels walking off (3.2 ps per km for 0.8 nm spacing at 4 ps/(nm·km)) while the accumulated dispersion is a third or less of standard fiber’s. (3) DCF: 20 km at −85 ps/(nm·km) cancels the 1700 ps/nm of the span, at the cost of 10 dB of extra loss, made up by the amplifier. (4) Coherent detection with digital equalisation undoes dispersion in the receiver, so new links use plain standard fiber.

Evaluation. At 10 Gbit/s the receiver tolerates about 1000 ps/nm, so an uncompensated 1550 nm span is limited to about 1000/17 ≈ 59 km; with DCF or digital compensation the reach becomes thousands of kilometres. At 1310 nm the dispersion would allow long spans, but 35 dB per 100 km with no practical amplifier makes repeaters necessary every 50 to 60 km.

Conclusion. Loss can be fixed only by amplification, and the amplifier works at 1550 nm; dispersion can be fixed by fiber design or signal processing. So the long-haul industry chose 1550 nm and manages its dispersion.

A 400 km system, both ways. At 1550 nm: four spans of 100 km, 20 dB each, with three in-line EDFAs and DCF (or a coherent receiver) for the 6800 ps/nm in total. At 1310 nm with a 0 dBm launch and a −28 dBm receiver: each regenerator section can be 28 ÷ 0.35 = 80 km, so five sections and four electronic regenerators, each tied to one bit rate and one channel. The amplified 1550 nm system can later carry many more WDM channels through the same amplifiers.

Role of the water peak. In older fiber the OH⁻ band near 1383 nm, about 1 dB/km or more, separated the two windows; low-water-peak fiber now makes the whole 1260 to 1625 nm range usable for coarse WDM in metro links, where spans are short and dispersion matters less.
Check. Loss saving: (0.35 − 0.20) × 100 = 15 dB = 35 − 20. Dispersion: 17 × 100 × 0.1 = 170 ps, and DCF length 1700/85 = 20 km.

bank.q: Explain stimulated Brillouin and stimulated Raman scattering in optical fibers. Compare their mechanisms, directions, shifts and thresholds, evaluate both thresholds for an 80 km span, and state how each affects a WDM link.
outline: Inelastic scattering, Stokes wave, threshold behaviour
SBS: electrostriction, acoustic grating, backward, about 11 GHz, narrow band
SRS: optical phonons, about 13 THz, broad band
L<sub>eff</sub> and threshold formulas with numbers
Effects on WDM and remedies
answer: Common idea. Both are inelastic: a signal photon gives part of its energy to the glass as a phonon and leaves as a lower-frequency Stokes photon. At low power this is weak and spontaneous; above a threshold the Stokes wave is amplified exponentially by the signal and takes a large share of its power.

SBS. The signal and a backward Stokes wave interfere; the moving intensity pattern compresses the glass by electrostriction and drives an acoustic wave. That wave is a moving Bragg grating that reflects more signal backward, Doppler-shifted down by νB = 2nvA/λ = 2 × 1.45 × 5960 ÷ 1.55 × 10⁻⁶ = 11.2 GHz. The gain bandwidth is only 20 to 50 MHz, set by the short life of the acoustic phonon.

SRS. The signal scatters off molecular vibrations of silica (optical phonons). The shift is about 13 THz (about 100 nm at 1550 nm), the gain band about 40 THz wide, and the Stokes wave grows mainly forward with the signal. The Raman gain coefficient is about 700 times smaller than the Brillouin one.

answer.text: Thresholds for an 80 km span (0.2 dB/km, Aeff = 80 µm², gB = 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m/W, gR = 7 × 10⁻¹⁴ m/W):

answer: Effects on a WDM link. SBS: each channel’s band lies inside one Brillouin gain band, so each channel is limited separately; above about 1.6 mW the extra launch power is reflected toward the transmitter, adding noise and possibly destabilising the laser. SRS: the Raman band covers the whole C-band, so short-wavelength channels pump long-wavelength ones; the spectrum tilts and channels exchange crosstalk, and the limit is on the total power.

Remedies. For SBS: dither or phase-modulate the laser so its spectrum is GHz wide (the empirical threshold 4.4 × 10⁻³ d²λ²αdBν grows with the source bandwidth ν: 68 mW for d = 8 µm, 0.2 dB/km and ν = 0.5 GHz), or use a larger Aeff. For SRS: limit total power, use gain-flattening and pre-emphasis of channel powers, and space channels sensibly.
Useful sides. Raman amplifiers pump the transmission fiber 13 THz above the signal; Brillouin sensors read strain and temperature from shifts of νB.

Empirical forms at another wavelength. At 1.31 µm with 0.35 dB/km and the same 8 µm core and 0.5 GHz source, PB = 4.4 × 10⁻³ × 64 × 1.716 × 0.35 × 0.5 = 85 mW and PR = 5.9 × 10⁻² × 64 × 1.31 × 0.35 = 1.73 W. Higher loss means a shorter effective length and so higher thresholds.
Check. Ratio of thresholds 0.86 W ÷ 1.59 mW = 541; from the formulas (16/21) × (5 × 10⁻¹¹ / 7 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 0.762 × 714 = 544, the same within rounding.

glossary.def: The fall of optical power with distance along a fiber, quoted as a coefficient in dB per kilometre.
A logarithmic power ratio, 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁), used so that cascaded losses add instead of multiply.
An absolute power level referred to 1 mW, so 0 dBm = 1 mW and −3 dBm ≈ 0.5 mW.
A wavelength band where fiber loss is low, notably around 850 nm, 1310 nm and 1550 nm.
Absorption caused by the silica network itself, through ultraviolet electronic transitions and infrared vibrational transitions.
Absorption caused by impurities in the glass, chiefly OH⁻ ions and transition-metal ions.
The strongest absorption band of the hydroxyl ion, near 1383 nm; weaker OH⁻ peaks lie near 950 and 720 nm, with a combination band near 1240 nm.
Fiber drawn from a dried preform so that the 1383 nm OH⁻ peak falls to about the 1310 nm loss, making 1260 to 1625 nm usable.
Scattering from density fluctuations much smaller than the wavelength, with loss proportional to 1/λ⁴.
Scattering from defects or bubbles comparable to the wavelength, with a much weaker wavelength dependence than Rayleigh scattering.
Loss caused by curving the whole fiber to a small radius, so the field on the outside of the bend radiates away.
Loss caused by small random kinks along the fiber axis, usually from cabling or coating stress.
The bend radius below which bending loss rises sharply; about 3n₁²λ/[4π(n₁² − n₂²)<sup>3/2</sup>] for multimode fiber and a few centimetres for single-mode fiber at 1550 nm.
One field pattern that can travel along the fiber, with its own propagation constant and group velocity.
Pulse spreading in multimode fiber because different modes take different paths and arrive at different times.
Multimode fiber whose core index decreases smoothly from the axis, equalising modal delays.
Pulse spreading because the group velocity depends on wavelength; measured in ps/(nm·km).
The part of chromatic dispersion coming from the wavelength dependence of the glass refractive index.
The part of chromatic dispersion coming from the way the mode's propagation constant depends on wavelength in a given core geometry.
The wavelength at which material and waveguide dispersion cancel; about 1310 nm for standard single-mode fiber, while silica’s material zero alone is near 1270 nm.
Random delay between the two polarization modes of a real, slightly non-circular fiber; grows as the square root of length.
The arrival-time difference between the two polarization modes, in picoseconds.
Fiber designed so that its zero-dispersion wavelength falls at 1550 nm, in the lowest-loss window.
Fiber with large negative dispersion, spliced in to cancel the accumulated positive dispersion of a link.
The area A<sub>eff</sub> over which the mode power is effectively spread, about 80 µm² in standard single-mode fiber; it sets the intensity and so the nonlinear thresholds.
Backward scattering from a light-driven acoustic wave, shifted down by about 11 GHz at 1550 nm, with a threshold of a few milliwatts for a narrow-line source.
Scattering from molecular vibrations, shifted down by about 13 THz, with a threshold near 1 W in one channel; useful for amplification but a source of crosstalk in WDM.
The length L<sub>eff</sub> = (1 − e<sup>−αL</sup>)/α over which the signal is strong enough to drive nonlinear effects; about 21 km for a long span at 0.2 dB/km.
The index difference δn between the two principal polarization axes of a fiber; it sets the beat length λ/δn.
Fiber with a small dispersion, about 2 to 6 ps/(nm·km), across the 1550 nm band, so WDM channels walk off and four-wave mixing stays weak.
